Governance Framework for Schools in
New Zealand
Introduction
This set of sample policies has been based on the work of John Carver and his Policy
Governance model. Our recommended governance framework for boards has the
following features:
The framework is informed by a researched body of knowledge on governance.
The policies are designed to work together as a suite rather than as separate
items.
The model introduces the notion of "ownership" of the school and that the
board's primary responsibility is to the owners.
We define the owners as being the Crown as the legal owners and the
community of people that the school serves both currently and in the future as
the moral owners.
The policies work collectively to define the role of the board and the relationship
between the board and principal.
The policies seek to focus the boards' role on governance and the principal's
role on leading and managing the school.
The intention of this set of policies is that the principal and staff are freed to use
their creativity and ideas to create exciting learning environments to meet the
expectations of the board who are representing the interests of the owners, and
within the limits set by the board.
The policies recognise that the principal is a part of and not separate from the
board and therefore will contribute as an equal with other board members to the
work of the board. However, there is also a point where the principal and their
staff take over the work of leading the school to obtaining the boards reflection
of the owners' wishes.
1
61

What is Governance?
In the case of schools, governance is the system for ensuring on behalf of its owners
(the Crown and community) that a school makes the difference it is supposed to make
for young people and the community, within the limits of reasonableness, ethics,
prudence and lawfulness (Gray 2020).
This is done by focusing on strategic leadership rather than administrative details.
The board sets clear policies articulating the Impacts the board wants to have,
Operational Expectations for the principal (the boundaries within which the principal
must operate), the Board-Management Relationship, and the Governance Culture
(processes) - to ensure effectiveness and accountability.
This model emphasizes the board's role in setting vision and policy, delegating
authority, and monitoring performance, rather than being involved in day-to-day
operations.
What are policies?
A policy is a formal statement of principles that guide decision making.
Policies are established by the board and define desired outcomes, constraints, and
governance processes. They provide clear direction and boundaries for the
organization, ensuring that the board's outcomes (Impacts) and expectations are met
while allowing the management the flexibility to decide on the methods to achieve
these expectations and outcomes.
The board exercises its role through its policies and so its policy framework is an
important document that all board members should be familiar with.
Nested Policies
This policy framework has a nested policy structure starting with a global policy for
each of the 4 main policy areas and then drilling down into more detail.
The numbering system reflects the nested nature of the policies.
It is for the board to decide how much detail they wish to determine policy and at what
point they wish to leave things to the principal to make any reasonable interpretation
of the written policy.
Global Policies are written to give the boards global expectation in a particular area so
that if some unforeseen event occurred for which there is no policy it may well be
covered by the global policy.

Impact Policies
Impact policies should reflect the expectations of the owners that for New
Zealand state and state integrated schools include the Crown and the
local community feeding into the school.
Impact policies should be stated as results (for students as intended
beneficiaries) - not activities, or efforts. They must describe what it is the
principal's job to accomplish (not board's philosophy or world view).
They should not be concerned about measurement (for the principal to
make any reasonable interpretation).
The impact policies need to be in place before the board can develop a
strategic plan.
The impact policies below reflect the wishes of the Crown owners as
expressed in s5(4) Education and Training Act 2020.
The school board needs to define its community and form a connection so
that it can reflect their wishes in their Impact Policies.
These policies could be called Ends policies, Results policies
We need to consider a 'toolkit' to help boards develop their impact policies
and show how to connect to their strategic planning.
1 Global Impact Policy
Each student will be enabled to develop their personality, talents and abilities to
fullest potential, and participate as responsible, informed, active and critical
citizens of the local, national and global communities in which they live - in a
learning community characterised by respect for everyone's rights and Te Tiriti o
Waitangi.
1.1
Fulfilment of Educational Potential
Each student has developed, to a level suitable for a successful transition to the
next stage of their lives,
a) resilience, determination, confidence, and creative and critical thinking,
b) good social skills and the ability to form good relationships,
c) participation in community life and fulfilment of civic and social
responsibilities,
d) preparedness for work,
e) appreciation of the importance of-
6
66

i.
the inclusion of different groups and persons with different personal
characteristics:
ii. diversity, cultural knowledge, identity, and the different official
languages:
iii. Te Tiriti o Waitangi and te reo Mãori (ETA S 5(4)
1.2 Experience of being in a Learning Community
All members of the learning community value learning and human rights
and support the learning and rights of others. Each student experiences
respect for their rights to a suitable education, physical and emotional
safety, non-discrimination, and other rights.
1.3 Respect for Te Tiriti o Waitangi
Students acknowledge, understand and respect:
New Zealand's bicultural heritage and the place of Te Tiriti as the founding
document in the constitution.
governance of New Zealand under the Crown;
Mãori rights and interests under Article 2;
citizenship equality under Article 3.

Board-Management Relationship Policies
Linking governance to the principal
2 Global Board-Management Relationship Policy
2.1 Board authority
A board is responsible for the governance of the school, including setting the
policies by which the school is to be controlled and managed. Only officially
passed motions of the board are binding on the principal.
2.1.1 Rests with the Board
Decisions or instructions of individual board members, officers, or
committees are not binding on the principal except in rare instances when
the board has specifically authorised such exercise of authority.
2.1.2 Requests of Principal need authorisation of the board
In the case of board members or committees requesting information or
assistance without board authorisation, the principal can refuse such
requests that require, in the principal's opinion, a material amount of staff
time or funds, or are disruptive.
2.2 Accountability of the Principal
The principal is the board's only link to the operation of the school, so that all
authority and accountability of staff is through the principal.
2.2.1 Exclusively
The board will never give instructions to persons who report directly or
indirectly to the principal.
2.2.2 Only Principal manages staff
The board will not manage, either formally or informally, any staff other than
the principal.
8
68

2.2.3 The principal is accountable for school performance
The board will view principal performance as identical to school
performance, in so far as it is reasonable to do so, so that school
accomplishment of board-stated Impacts and within operational
expectations will be viewed as successful principal performance.
2.3 Delegation to the Principal
The board will instruct the principal through written policies that prescribe
the organisational Impacts to be achieved, broad operational expectations
and organisational situations and actions to be avoided, allowing the
principal to use any reasonable interpretation of these policies.
2.3.1 Delegation to the Principal for achieving Impacts
Impact policies will be developed by the board instructing the principal
to achieve specified results, for all students, within resources available
to the board.
2.3.2 Delegations to the Principal will include delegations
The board's Operational Expectation policies will describe those
practices, activities, decisions, and circumstances that would be
unacceptable to the board even if they were to be effective. Outside of
these operational expectations the principal has freedom to use their
discretion in exercising their delegations.
2.3.3 Reasonable Interpretation
As long as the principal uses any reasonable interpretation of the
board's Impact and Operational Expectation policies, the principal is
authorised to establish all further policies, make all decisions, take all
actions, establish all practices, and pursue all activities. Such decisions
of the principal shall have full force and authority as if decided by the
board.
2.3.4 Changing delegations
The board may change its Impact and Operational Expectation policies,
thereby shifting the boundary between board and principal decision-
making.
9
69

2.4 Monitoring Principal Performance
Systematic and rigorous monitoring of principal performance will be solely
against the only expected principal job outputs: organisational
accomplishment of board policies on Impacts and organisational operation
within the boundaries established in board policies on Operational
Expectations.
2.4.1 Purpose of Monitoring
Monitoring is simply to determine the degree to which board policies are
being met. Information that does not do this will not be considered to be
monitoring information.
2.4.2 Sources of information
The board will acquire monitoring information by one or more of three
methods:
a) By internal report, in which the principal discloses interpretations and
compliance information to the board
b) By external report, in which an external, disinterested third party
selected by the board assesses compliance with board policies
c) By direct board inspection, in which a designated member or
members of the board assess compliance with the appropriate policy
criteria.
2.4.3 Board Judgements
In every case, the board will judge (a) the reasonableness of the principal's
interpretation and (b) whether data demonstrates accomplishment of the
interpretation.
2.4.4 Reasonable Interpretation
The standard of compliance shall be any reasonable principal
interpretation of the board policy being monitored. The board is the final
arbiter of reasonableness but will always judge with a "reasonable
person" test rather than with an interpretation favored by board members
or by the board as a whole.
10
70

2.4.5 Frequency of Policy Monitoring
All policies that instruct the principal will be monitored at a frequency and
by a method chosen by the board. The board can monitor any policy at
any time by any method, but will ordinarily depend on a routine schedule:

Operational Expectation Policies
3 Global Operational Expectation Policy
The principal shall not cause or allow any school practice, activity,
decision, or circumstance that is either unlawful, imprudent, or in
violation of their professional standards or commonly accepted
business ethics and practices.
3.1 Expectations with students
The school board has an obligation to ensure the wellbeing of children in our care, so
they belong, thrive, and achieve. We are committed to the prevention of child abuse
and neglect and to the protection of all children. The safety and wellbeing of the child
is our top priority. Advice will be sought through appropriate agencies in all cases of
suspected or alleged abuse. In relation to students, the principal shall not cause
or allow conditions, procedures, or decisions that are contrary to their rights,
unsafe, untimely, undignified, or unnecessarily intrusive.
3.1.1 Child Safety
The principal will not fail to establish procedures that all employees and school
contractors are aware of with respect to child safety that comply with legislation
and recognised best practice so that any person in the school who believes that
any child or young person who have been or are at risk of being harmed (whether
physically, emotionally, or sexually) ill-treated, abused, neglected, or deprived
must follow school procedures and report to a senior leader or the school
guidance counsellor who may choose to report the matter local police or Oranga
Tamariki.
3.1.2 Reducing distress and minimising restraint
The principal shall not fail to ensure that the Education (Physical Restraint) Rules
2023, and related guide on understanding distress and minimising restraint, are
understood and followed by staff.
3.2 Expectations with staff
In relation to staff, the principal will not fail to observe current employment
legislation and may not cause or allow conditions that are inconsistent with
public sector expectations of a "good employer" or are unfair, undignified,
disorganised, or unclear.
12
72

3.2.1 Good Faith
The principal will maintain a position of good faith in all interactions with
staff. The principal shall not fail to:
Ensure that employees are not discriminated against on other than
clearly job- related, individual performance or qualifications.
Ensure all employees their rights to personal dignity, safety and access
to an approved and fair internal grievance process and
Ensure that staff are aware of their responsibilities as employees of the
school to their colleagues and to their employer.
Provide Protected Disclosure procedures.
3.2.2 EEO
The principal shall not fail to develop and execute an EEO programme, that is
available to all employees and report to the board on its implementation and
compliance.
3.2.3 Remuneration and Benefits
The principal should not fail to have employment agreement for all
employees. If a position is covered by a collective agreement the provisions
that apply to that position as described in the collective agreement must be
applied. For positions for which there is not a collective agreement available
that an individual agreement is in place.
3.2.4 Engagement of Consultants, Contractors and volunteers
The principal may not enter into any grant or contract arrangements that fail
to emphasise primarily the meeting of Impacts and, secondarily, the
avoidance of unacceptable means.
3.3 Financial Conditions & Activity
In relation to the actual, ongoing financial conditions and activities, the
principal shall not cause or allow the development of financial jeopardy or
material deviation of actual expenditures from board priorities established in
Impact Policies
3.3.1 Financial Planning/Budgeting
Budgeting shall not fail to reflect the board's Impact policies, risk financial
jeopardy nor fail to show a generally acceptable level of foresight. Thus, the
budget should not neglect to:
Reflect the impacts sought by the board.
13
73

Reflect the priorities as established by the board.
Comply with the board's requirement of a balanced budget.
Ensure adequate working capital.
Demonstrate an appropriate degree of conservatism in all estimates
3.3.2 Financial Condition
The financial viability of the organisation must be protected at all times. Therefore,
the principal shall not:
a. Incur unauthorised debt.
b. Violate generally accepted accounting practices or principles.
C. Use tagged funds for purposes other than those approved.
d. Spend more funds than have been allocated in the fiscal year.
e. Fail to ensure all money owed to the school is collected in a timely manner.
f. Fail to make timely payment to staff and other creditors
g. Sell or purchase unauthorised property.
h. Spend on single items beyond a board-established limit.
i.
Fail to ensure that all relevant government returns are completed on time.
j.
Fail to ensure that no one person has complete authority over the school's
financial transactions.
k. Make any purchase:
1. Of over $xxxx without having obtained comparative prices and
quality.
2. Of over $xxxx without an adequate review on ongoing costs, value
and reliability
3.3.3 Impact Focus of Grants or Contracts
The principal may not enter into any grant or contract arrangements that fail
to emphasise primarily the meeting of Impacts and, secondarily, the
avoidance of unacceptable means.
3.4 Asset Protection
The principal shall not cause or allow school assets to be unprotected,
inadequately maintained, or unnecessarily risked. Therefore, the Principal may
not:
a) Fail to insure assets.
b) Allow unauthorised personnel to handle funds or school property.
c) Subject plant and equipment to improper wear and tear or insufficient
maintenance or inappropriate use.
d) Fail to ensure the implementation of the 10-year property maintenance plan
14
74

e) Fail to protect intellectual property, information and files from loss or
significant damage or unauthorised access or duplication.
f) Receive, process or disburse funds under controls that are insufficient to
meet the board-appointed auditor's standards.
g) Invest or hold operating capital in insecure accounts, or in non-interest
bearing accounts except where necessary to facilitate ease in operational
transactions.
3.5 Communication and Support to the Board
The principal shall not cause or allow the board to be uninformed or
unsupported in its work.
3.6 Emergency Principal Succession
To protect the board from sudden loss of Principal services, the principal shall
not permit there to be fewer than two other senior managers sufficiently familiar
with board and Principal issues and processes to enable either to take over with
reasonable proficiency as an interim successor.
3.7 Health & Safety
Students and staff shall have a safe physical and emotional learning
environment. The board recognises that everyone is responsible for Health &
Safety and that the board, in its role as the PCBU, has the primary
responsibility for the health, safety and wellbeing of workers but, that the board
expects the principal and staff to design and implement a Health and Safety
system that protects all employees, students, volunteers, contractors and
visitors to the school. The principal will provide the board with regular reports to
give the board assurance that the school is a safe physically and emotionally
place for all students and staff.
3.7.1 Workers Participation
The Health & Safety System will ensure workers are regularly made aware of
opportunities to participate in improving health and safety including through
health and safety representatives and the health and safety committee.
The principal will also ensure workers can raise any health and safety concerns
directly with them.
15
75

3.7.2 Managing Risk
The Health & Safety System will include clearly documented procedures
for identifying and reporting hazards and risk and systems for managing
those risks that may include mitigation or rectification.
3.7.3 Property and Equipment
The principal must have systems that ensure that all property and
equipment are well-maintained and are safe condition to use.
3.7.4 Emergency Plans including evacuations
The Health and Safety System will include plans for responding to
emergencies affecting the school, including weather related events,
natural disasters and other threats to health and life. The principal is
delegated the authority to deal with all aspects of such events including
decisions to close the school if it is deemed unsafe to remain open.
3.7.5 Health and Wellbeing
The principal will engage closely with staff and students to support a
proactive approach to health and wellbeing with specific health and well-
being programmes.
3.7.6 Induction, training and information
The principal will not fail to ensure that a programme of induction is
provided for all new employees and that staff receive professional
development in health and safety that will strengthen the capability of staff
to maintain a safe and happy work environment including how to keep
themselves as safe as possible.
3.7.7 EOTC provisions
The principal will not fail to ensure that the Health & Safety System will
include specific systems for ensuring that all EOTC events including
sports events are safe for all participants and appropriately supervised.
3.8 Concerns and complaints
The principal shall not fail to ensure robust procedures to ensure
complaints, concerns and incidents are attended to promptly, fairly,
respectfully and professionally, and seek to bring effective resolution to all
parties concerned.
3.8.1. The principal shall not fail to ensure:

76

Governance Culture Policies
Defining the Board's Job
4 Global Governance Culture Policy
The purpose of the board, on behalf of the Crown and community, is
to see to it that the school (a) achieves its desired results for its
students (as described in its Impact policies) within the resourcing
available to it, (b) avoids unacceptable actions and situations (as
prohibited in board Operational Expectation policies) while fulfilling its
commitment to Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
4.1 Governing Style
The board emphasises strategic leadership rather than administrative
details, has a clear distinction of board and staff roles (as described in its
Board - Management Relationships policies), concentrates on the future
rather than the past or present, and is pro-active rather than reactive.
4.1.1 Group responsibility
The board will cultivate a sense of group responsibility. All members of the board
have equal standing, voice, vote and accountability. The board, not the staff, will
be responsible for excellence in governing. The board will be the initiator of policy,
not merely a reactor to staff initiatives. Although individual board members may
have expert knowledge on matters being discussed the decision rests with the
whole board.
4.1.2 Direction through policy
The board will direct, control, and inspire the school staff through the careful
establishment of broad written policies reflecting the board's values and
perspectives.
The board's written policies realistically address the broadest levels of all
organisational decisions and situations:
Impact - the impacts, benefits, outcomes; recipients, beneficiaries, impacted
groups; and their relative worth in cost or priority
18
78

Operational Expectations - constraints on executive authority that establish
the prudence and ethics boundaries within which all executive
activity and decisions must take place
Governance Culture - specification of how the board conceives, carries out,
and monitors its own task
Board-Management Relationship - how power is delegated, and its proper
use monitored, the principal's role, authority, and accountability
4.1.3 Board Discipline
Board members are aware of and comply with the government mandated
code of conduct for school board members. The board will enforce upon
itself whatever discipline is needed to govern with excellence and
adherence to board policies. Discipline will apply to matters such as
attendance, preparation for meetings, policymaking principles, respect of
roles, and ensuring the continuance of governance capability.
4.1.4 Board Continuity &Development
Continual board development will include induction of new board members
as well as succession planning to ensure continuity in the board's
governance process and periodic board discussion of process
improvement.
4.1.5 Board self-monitoring
Self-monitoring will include comparison of board activity and discipline to
policies in the Governance Culture and Board-Management Relationship
categories.
4.2 Board's Role
The board's role is to provide leadership by reflecting the agreed
aspirations and expectations of the school community and the Crown in
board policy. The board is accountable to the community and the Crown on
these key roles and will regularly report on progress and compliance.
The board is a continuous entity, regardless of changes in membership,
and its policies and decisions continue to exist until such time as they are
rescinded or revoked.
19
79

4.2.1 Connection to Owners
The board will gain an understanding of Crown expectation as expressed in
legislation and of the values and aspirations of their community, to
incorporate these in board policy.
4.2.2 Monitoring & Assurance
The board will monitor the effect of its policies through principal reports,
third-party monitoring and, where warranted, direct inspection, in order to
be assured of successful school performance on Impacts and Operational
Expectations.
4.2.3 Board Work Plan
To fulfill its role the board will follow a work plan that
(a) completes a re-exploration of Impact policies annually,
(b) continually improves board performance through board education and
enriched input and deliberation and
(c) reviews other policies as appropriate.
1. The cycle will conclude each year on the last day of December so
that administrative planning and budgeting can be based on
accomplishing the annual implementation plan.
2. The cycle will start with the board's development of its agenda for
the next year.
a. Consultations with selected groups in the ownership, or other
methods of gaining ownership input, will be determined and
arranged in the first quarter, to be held during the balance of
the year.
b. Governance education and education related to ends
determination (presentations by futurists, demographers,
advocacy groups, staff, and so on) will be arranged in the
first quarter, to be held during the balance of the year.
C. A board member may recommend or request an item for
board discussion by submitting the item to the Presiding
Member no later than five days before the board meeting.
3. Throughout the year, the board will attend to consent agenda items
as expeditiously as possible.
20
80

ensure that formal proposals before the board are clearly stated for final
board consideration, and that resulting board decisions are clearly
stated (and indicated in minutes); and authorises the presiding member
to facilitate accordingly.
4.5 Presiding Member's Role
The presiding member (PM) chairs the board meetings and is authorised to
carry out those duties that are delegated by the board. The PM ensures the
integrity of the board's process and, where authorized, represents the
board to outside parties..
4.5.1 Presiding Member's Role
The presiding members role is to oversee the work of the board. The
PM's directs the board to behave consistently with its own policies,
rules and those legitimately imposed upon it from outside the school.
a)
Meetings will focus solely on issues that clearly belong to the board,
to determine or monitor according to board policy.
b)
Information that is neither for monitoring performance nor for board
decisions will not be discussed or tabled at board meetings.
c)
Deliberations by the board will be fair, open, and thorough but also
timely, orderly, and kept to the point.
4.5.2 Presiding Member's Authority
The PM has the authority to make decisions under the board policies on
Governance Culture and Board-Management Relationship as long as they
can be shown to be reasonable interpretation of the policies except for:
(a) The employment or termination of the principal and
(b) Areas where the board specifically delegates portions of this authority to
others.
4.5.2.1
The PM shall preside over meetings of the board with all the
commonly accepted powers of that position.
4.5.2.2
Except as delegated by the board the PM has no authority to
supervise or direct the principal.
4.5.2.3
The PM may as delegated represent the board to outside parties in
announcing board decisions and confirming the process being
undertaken by the school in urgent or critical matters.
22
82

4.5.2.4
Under the authority of the board the PM may delegate any part or
all of these responsibilities .
4.6 Board Secretary
The role of the board secretary is to ensure the integrity of the board's
documents.
4.6.1 Board Secretary's Role
While the formal contractual arrangements may sensibly be handled by the
principal, the board secretary is accountable to the board (and their key
functional relationship is with its presiding member).
The assigned result is to see to it that all board documents and filings are
accurate and timely, including the following:
a) Meeting minutes that are an official record of the board's process and actions,
particularly its resolutions and adoption of policies (board policies cannot be
shown to have been created or altered except through the authority of the
minutes).
b) A centrally-organised, accessible and visible collection of current policies, with
clear indication of adoption date by the board.
c) Central filing of formal board correspondence.
d) Up-to-date board membership records, including ensuring and filing eligibility
declarations, a board membership register (that records phone and email
contacts, formal position on the board, membership type (elected, selected, co-
opted, ex officio) date membership started, date member left board, expiry of
term), and ensuring new board members (including the principal) and new

4.7 Board Committee Principles
Board committees are to be used sparingly, preferably as adhoc
committees to preserve the board functioning as a whole when other
methods have been deemed inadequate and so as never to interfere with
delegation from board to principal.
This policy applies to any group that is formed by board decision, whether
or not it is called a committee. A board committee may include non-board

members but must include at least one board member. It does not apply to
committees formed under the authority of the principal.
A board committee shall be given a written terms of reference that describe
constitution, aims and delegations.
4.7.1 Board Committee Role
Board committees are to help the board do its job, never to advise or carry
out the work of staff. Committees ordinarily will assist the board by
preparing policy alternatives and implications for board deliberation. In
keeping with the board's broader focus, board committees will normally not
have direct dealings with current staff operations.
4.7.2 Board Committee Scope
Board committees may not speak or act for the board except when formally
given such authority for specific and time-limited purposes. Expectations
and authority will be carefully stated in order to prevent conflict with
authority delegated to the principal.
4.7.3 Board Committees Limit on Authority
Board committees cannot exercise authority over staff. The principal works
for the full board and will therefore not be required to obtain the approval of
a board committee before an executive action.
4.8 Cost of Governance
Because poor governance costs more than learning to govern well, the
board will invest in its governance capacity.
4.8.1 Resourcing the Board
Board skills, methods, and supports will be sufficient to ensure governing with
excellence.
1. Training and retraining will be used liberally to orient new members and
candidates for membership, as well as to maintain and increase existing
members' skills and understandings.
2. Outside monitoring assistance will be arranged so that the board can
exercise confident control over organisational performance. This includes
but is not limited to financial audit.
